stem.text: Consider the curve (x^2 - 4x + 1)(y^2 + 2y) = -6, for which dy/dx = -(x - 2)(y^2 + 2y)/((x^2 - 4x + 1)(y + 1)). The tangent line to the curve is vertical at a point in the fourth quadrant. What is the x-coordinate of that point?

worked_solution.text: A vertical tangent needs the denominator of dy/dx to be zero with the numerator nonzero. The denominator is zero when y = -1 or when x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0, that is x = 2 + sqrt(3) or x = 2 - sqrt(3).
At x = 2 + sqrt(3) or x = 2 - sqrt(3) the factor x^2 - 4x + 1 is 0, so the left side of the curve equation is 0, not -6. Neither x-value belongs to a point of the curve.
Substitute y = -1: y^2 + 2y = -1, so x^2 - 4x + 1 = 6 and x^2 - 4x - 5 = 0, which gives x = 5 or x = -1.
At (5, -1) the numerator is -(3)(-1) = 3, which is nonzero, so the tangent is vertical there. The point (5, -1) is in the fourth quadrant and (-1, -1) is in the third, so the x-coordinate is 5.
